title: Why Circuits Need Memory
excerpt: Every gate-only circuit you've built so far forgets its inputs the instant they change. Here's the feedback trick that lets a circuit remember, and why it doesn't collapse into an infinite loop.

content.text: Build a half adder. Feed it A = 1, B = 0 today, and A = 1, B = 0 again next year. You get SUM = 1, CARRY = 0 both times, no exceptions. Nothing in the circuit tracks what happened before, because nothing needs to. That single property, output depends only on current input, is both the strength and the ceiling of every gate-only circuit you've built so far.

body.text: Combinational Logic: A Pure Function of Its Inputs

content.text: Half adders, multiplexers, majority voters: all of them belong to a category called
. Formally, a combinational circuit computes a function

with no dependence on time. Change the inputs, wait one propagation delay, and the output settles. That's the entire lifecycle. Most of digital logic is combinational, and for pure computation (adders, comparators, decoders) that's all you'll ever need.

But a computer needs more than computation. It needs to count, hold a running total, remember which state a state machine is currently in, and store a byte long after the signal that produced it is gone. None of that is expressible as a pure function of the current inputs, because the whole point is that the output has to depend on something that isn't there anymore: history.

body.text: Why a Combinational Circuit Can't Remember

content.text: Take an AND gate feeding a NOT gate. At every instant its output is fully determined by its inputs at that instant. The moment an input changes, the previous value isn't stored anywhere, waiting to be read later. It's gone: not hidden, not cached, just absent from the circuit entirely. There's no wire, no node, nothing you could probe to recover what the input used to be.

That's fine for an adder, useless for anything that has to hold a value once the thing that set it disappears: a light switch that stays on after you release the button, a counter that keeps its count after the clock tick that incremented it, a single bit of RAM. All three need a circuit whose output can stay fixed independent of what the inputs are doing right now.

body.text: The Trick: Route a Gate's Output Back Into Itself

content.text: Every circuit built so far flows one direction: inputs on the left, gates in the middle, outputs on the right, no wire ever loops back upstream. Sequential logic breaks that rule deliberately. Take a gate's output and wire it back into one of its own inputs (directly, or through a neighboring gate that loops back into it), and the gate's output stops being a pure function of its external inputs. It becomes a function of its own recent output too, because that old output is now literally one of the signals feeding it.

That's the whole idea behind every storage element in this section: the SR latch, the gated D latch, the D flip-flop. Different wiring, different rules for when the stored value can change, but every one of them is built from ordinary NAND or NOR gates arranged in a loop. There's no separate "memory gate" primitive underneath. It's the same gates you already know, just connected differently.

body.text: Why This Doesn't Blow Up Into an Infinite Loop

content.text: A feedback loop in software that recomputes a value from itself is usually a bug. In a digital circuit it isn't, because gates aren't instantaneous. Every gate has a small propagation delay, so a signal chasing itself around a loop doesn't recompute forever, it

. After a handful of gate delays the loop reaches a value that's consistent with itself, every gate's output matches what its inputs demand, and nothing changes further. That settling behavior is what makes the next three tutorials safe to build, and it's why simulating one of these circuits gate-by-gate always converges instead of spinning.
Three storage elements, built in order, each one fixing a specific problem with the last:

body.code:
SR latch        -> two cross-coupled NOR gates, the smallest circuit that stores a bit
                   (has one input combination that is genuinely forbidden)
Gated D latch   -> fixes the forbidden state by trading two inputs (S, R) for one (D)
                   (still reacts to a signal LEVEL, which causes race-through when chained)
D flip-flop     -> fixes race-through by reacting to a clock EDGE instead of a level
                   (this is what real registers and counters are built from)

content.text: By the end you'll know exactly what a register is made of, gate by gate, and why each design decision along the way was forced by a specific limitation of the one before it.
